I am 48 years old and have farmed in Quzhou County all my life. I never went to school, but I know this land, and I watch what my neighbors do. Here on the North China Plain, we always grow winter wheat followed by summer maize — that is the safest way to feed my family and earn some cash at the market. I have about 6 mu of good flat land. My wheat went into the ground last October, and now that spring has come I will top-dress it with fertilizer and irrigate it three times before the June harvest. I use an improved wheat variety — I saved the seeds from what I bought a few years back from the agricultural supply shop in town. Right after we harvest the wheat in early June, I will plant hybrid maize. I buy new hybrid maize seed every year — varieties like Denghai or Nongda — because everyone says hybrid seed gives the best yield, and I can see it with my own eyes in my fields. For fertilizer, I apply what the village extension agent and the shop recommend. For wheat, I put down about 15 kg of nitrogen per mu, plus about 7 kg of phosphorus and 4 kg of potassium from compound fertilizer. For maize, I use a bit less nitrogen, about 13 kg per mu, and roughly 4 kg of phosphorus and 3 kg of potassium. I irrigate from our well using border irrigation. The wheat needs three good irrigations — one now at the jointing stage, one at heading, and one at grain filling. The maize usually needs two irrigations in summer if the rains are not enough. I till the land with the rotary tiller before wheat planting in autumn, but for maize I plant no-till right after wheat harvest to save time and keep the soil moisture — that is what everyone in our village does now. For pests, I spray about three times on wheat and twice on maize — herbicide, insecticide, and sometimes fungicide when the wheat rust appears. If the weather is normal, I expect my wheat to yield about 950 kg per mu and the maize about 1,100 kg per mu.
